legendContentsJwt: every credential the reply carried, in the order they were minted — one row, however many that is
legendContentsOther: one credential: these protocols issue one thing per act, so the cell is the kind and nothing else
legendStateJwt: the state every member shares, or mixed when they differ — which they usually do, since an access token and the refresh token beside it have very different lifetimes. Hover for the breakdown
legendExpiresJwt: the first member to go, then the last — a set comes apart before it is finished, and the earlier instant is the one a refused call is about
legendUserJwt: username, as typed at the sign-in screen
legendUserOther: nothing: each of these has one name, and it is in Subject
legendPartySaml: the AudienceRestriction, or unrestricted when WS-Trust was given no AppliesTo
legendPartyTicket: the service the ticket is for; hover for the realm that issued it
legendDetailJwt: the ACCESS TOKEN's scope. The refresh token beside it deliberately carries a different one — what was authorized, rather than what this token can do — so the two disagree by design, and the set page shows each. A scope that became the audience is not on either
legendDetailSaml: whether the signature was written — an assertion that failed to sign still went out
legendDetailTicket: the enc-type it was sealed with
legendPresentedJwt: Bearer, or DPoP when cnf.jkt binds it to a key
legendPresentedSaml: bearer SubjectConfirmation; there is no holder-of-key form here
legendPresentedTicket: in a TGS-REQ (a TGT) or an AP-REQ (a service ticket)
legendJtiJwt: a set of one shows the jti and opens that credential's lineage; a group shows the set id and opens the set. The set id is this service's own handle on a reply — it is in no token, no client ever sees it, and it is not a claim
legendJtiTicket: none exists — a ticket has no identifier to quote, and the KDC keeps no handle on one
legendButtonJwt: Revoke, or Revoke set on a group, which sends every revocable member through the same act one at a time. Nothing new is written: it is the same set of revoked jtis /oauth2/revoke writes to
legendButtonOther: there is none, and there is nothing it could do — see above
leadEverything: Everything this service has issued and still remembers: every JWT, every SAML assertion — whether WS-Trust issued it or a WS-Federation sign-in did — and every Kerberos ticket the KDC minted, in one table, newest first. One table rather than three because a WS-Federation sign-in that produced an ID Token and a SAML 1.1 assertion is one event, and three tables would leave it to be reassembled by comparing timestamps.
leadOneRow: One row is one issuance, not one credential. OAuth 2.0 and OIDC are the only protocols here that hand back several credentials at once — redeeming an authorization code returns an access token, a refresh token and an ID Token in a single reply, and response_type=id_token token returns two in one fragment — so those are drawn as one row saying what it contains, with a link to the set. Every other family issues one credential per act, so a SAML assertion, a Kerberos ticket and a SPIFFE SVID are each a set of one and look exactly as they always did. The grouping comes from an identifier the issuer stated at the moment it built the reply, never from guessing that two rows near each other in time belong together: two people redeeming two codes at the same client in the same millisecond produce six credentials that agree on every column below, and a table that merged them would report a reply nobody ever received.
leadRefreshing: Refreshing makes a new set beside the old one, not a bigger one. A set is one response: it has one issued instant and one grant, which a row that grew all afternoon could not have. What joins the generations of a grant is the refresh lineage, and that is drawn — as a picture, back to the issuance the whole line rests on — on each credential's own page.
leadOnlyJwts: Only the JWTs can be invalidated. Revoking one here is the SAME operation RFC 7009's /oauth2/revoke performs — there is one set of revoked jtis in this service, not one per page. So a token revoked here immediately introspects as inactive at /oauth2/introspect, is refused by /oauth2/userinfo with invalid_token, and fails the refresh grant with invalid_grant. Two sets would each look correct on their own and never see each other, which is a debugging session with no error message anywhere in it.
leadAssertionButton: An assertion, a ticket and an SVID have a button since 2026-09-05, and pressing it changes nothing out there. That is not a contradiction and the distinction is the whole of what this row means: what this service knows and what a relying party will honour are two different claims. Nothing consults this service when one of these is presented — an assertion is valid because its signature verifies and its Conditions hold, a ticket because the service it names can decrypt it with a key it already has, an SVID because it chains to a bundle — so a revocation here reaches none of them and never will. What it does is record that this identity provider has disowned the credential, which is what a sign-out has to be able to say, what CAEP can carry to a receiver that subscribed, and what SAML Single Logout can carry for an assertion issued through a browser profile. A WS-Trust assertion has neither channel and the mark is the whole of what exists for it — which is exactly why it is worth having, because otherwise the answer to "did you sign them out" would depend on which endpoint issued the credential. The button says (record only) and its tooltip says this again, so it cannot be pressed by somebody who thinks it did more.
labelTarget: A jti, or paste the whole token
pasting: Pasting a token is read for its jti and the signature is not checked, which is safe: a forged token yields a jti this service never issued, and revoking one of those invalidates nothing. To undo a revocation, use the Restore button in the table — a NON-SPEC operation no real authorization server can offer, kept because otherwise getting back to a working token means restarting this service.
labelSubject: Everything for one subject or username
sessionBefore: Narrowed to what was issued on the browser sign-on session {session}, which is how
sessionAfter: links here. Only credentials issued UNDER a session carry one, so an assertion, a Kerberos ticket, a token from either direct grant and anything an RFC 8693 exchange produced are absent by construction rather than missing — that is a fact about the credential and not a gap in the recording.
familyAndKind: Family and Kind narrow together: choosing a family and a kind from a different one matches nothing, which is what an empty table below then means.
filterMatchesSet: A filter matches a set when any credential in it matches. Asking for id_token answers with the replies that contain an ID Token — the access token and the refresh token that came back with it are still on the row, because they are part of the same reply. The same goes for State: a set holding an expired access token and a valid refresh token is found by both, and its State column reads mixed rather than picking one.
setsOnPage: , of which sets {first}–{last} are on this page ({page} of {pages})
heldInTotal: ; {sets} set(s) over {credentials} credential(s) held in total —
perFamilyBefore: . The per-family figures are credentials, not sets, so that they agree with the count on
perFamilyAfter: — two pages of one console disagreeing about how much has been issued is worse than one line carrying both units and saying which is which. Paging is by SET, so a page is a whole number of replies rather than a boundary drawn through the middle of one. Newest first, so page 1 is what somebody is most likely to be debugging. Only the claims and the facts below are kept, never the signed token, the assertion XML or the ticket: a page rendering a thousand live credentials in a form a browser will display is a page that leaks them, and the jti is all any button here needs.
columnsLead: Three families in one table, so most columns answer a slightly different question depending on the row. Rather than leave that to be inferred:
oid4vciBefore: OID4VCI credentials are not in this table. They are recorded and counted on
oid4vciAfter: and listed nowhere. That is a gap rather than a principle — a credential is as much an issued artifact as an assertion is — and it is named here so that "everything this service has issued" above is read as the three families it says and not as four.
pagingJson: Paging is ?page= and ?per= (at most {max} sets a page), and both work with ?format=json — where the reply carries page, pages and matched, so a test can walk the whole list without guessing when it has reached the end. Those three count SETS, which is what this list is; matchedCredentials and held are the same figures in credentials. The sets are in sets, each carrying its members — and issued is the same members flattened, so a caller written against the older per-credential shape reads exactly what it read and the two cannot disagree, because one is built out of the other. Every button on this page acts on a jti or a setKey and never on a row number, so a revocation between two clicks cannot make the wrong token the target — the most it can do is shift a row onto another page.
contentsTitle: {n} credentials came back in one reply
contentsTitleEnd: . Every one of them is on the set page, with its own identifier, its own expiry and its own button.
unsignedTitle: Signing threw and the assertion went out unsigned rather than not at all, so that a relying party can reject it for the right reason. The log line says what failed.
signedTitle: An enveloped XML signature over the assertion, its reference naming the ID (SAML 2.0) or the AssertionID (SAML 1.1).
etypeTitle: The enc-type the ticket and its session key were sealed with.
unrestrictedTitle: This assertion carries no AudienceRestriction — WS-Trust was asked to Issue with no AppliesTo. Any relying party may accept it, which is the thing an audience restriction exists to prevent, so it is named here rather than shown as a dash.
bearerTitle: Both builders write a bearer SubjectConfirmation: whoever holds the assertion may present it. There is no holder-of-key confirmation here, so there is nothing for this column to distinguish between.
tgsReqTitle: A TGT goes back to the KDC in a TGS-REQ to get a service ticket. It is never presented to a service, which is why it is the Kerberos session rather than one use of one.
apReqTitle: A service ticket is presented to the service it names, in an AP-REQ — over raw Kerberos, or wrapped in SPNEGO over HTTP.
dpopTitle: Bound to a key: cnf.jkt is in the token and a DPoP proof over that key has to accompany it.
setNothingRevocable: Nothing in this set can be revoked: only access tokens, ID Tokens and refresh tokens can be, and the others are replies rather than credentials or carry no jti to act on.
restoreSetTitle: Un-revoke every revocable credential in this set. NON-SPEC — no real authorization server can undo a revocation.
revokeSetTitle: Revoke the {n} revocable credential(s) in this set in one act. Each one is revoked exactly as its own button would revoke it, into the same set of revoked jtis RFC 7009's /oauth2/revoke writes to.
expiryRangeTitle: The members of this set expire at different times. The first goes at {first} and the last at {last}; the set page says which is which.
setLinkTitle: The {n} credentials this one reply carried, each with its own identifier, expiry and button — and a link on to where each of them came from. The set id is this service's own handle on the reply: it is in no token, no client ever sees it, and it is not a claim.
mixedTitle: The members of this set are not all in the same state: {parts}. That is the ordinary case rather than a fault — an access token and the refresh token issued with it have very different lifetimes — so this column reports the disagreement instead of picking one. The set page has each member and its own state. Filtering by a state finds a set when ANY member holds it.
userNoneTitle: A SAML assertion names a Subject and a Kerberos ticket names a client principal. Neither carries a second, human-readable name beside it the way a JWT carries username beside sub, so the one name it has is in the Subject column.
noJtiTitle: This one carries no jti to act on — a signed UserInfo response has none, and the WS-Trust JWT is signed directly rather than through signJwt(). There is nothing to name in a revocation.
restoreArtifactTitle: Take this service's disavowal back. NON-SPEC, like every restore here.
revokeArtifactTitle: Mark it revoked IN THIS SERVICE'S OWN RECORD, which is the whole of what this can do and is worth doing. THE HOLDER WILL NOT BE TOLD BY THIS BUTTON: a relying party validates a SAML assertion's signature and its Conditions and asks nobody, a Kerberos service decrypts a ticket with a key it already has, and an X509-SVID chains to a bundle — so this credential goes on working out there until it expires. What the mark buys is that a global logout can say what it disowned, that CAEP can transmit it to a receiver that subscribed, and that SAML Single Logout can carry it for an assertion that came from a browser profile. A WS-Trust assertion has neither channel, and the mark is all there is.
restoreTokenTitle: Un-revoke it. NON-SPEC — no real authorization server can undo a revocation.
revokeTokenTitle: Revoke it. Introspection immediately reports it inactive, UserInfo refuses it with invalid_token, and the refresh grant fails with invalid_grant.
ticketNoIdTitle: A Kerberos ticket carries no identifier anybody can quote: no jti, no ID. It is named by its client, its service and when it was issued — the columns to the left — and the KDC keeps no handle on it either, because the KDC is stateless and the ticket is the state. With no identifier there is nothing to look a lineage up BY either, which is why this row has no link where the others do.
noIdTitle: This one carries no identifier — the signed UserInfo response has no jti, and the WS-Trust JWT is signed directly rather than through signJwt(). Nothing can be looked up by a name that does not exist.
lineageTitle: Where this credential came from: who it was issued to, in whose name, to reach what — and, if it came out of a token exchange, the credential handed in to get it and every generation behind that, back to the issuance the whole line rests on.
noSetBefore: This page draws the credentials that came back in ONE reply, and the way to it is the link in the last column of
noSetAfter: on any row that shows more than one. A row showing a single credential links to that credential's own lineage instead, because for one credential this page would be a click that added nothing.
setGrouped: {n} credentials came back in one reply, from the {grant} grant.
setOfOne: One credential, issued on its own.
setLeadBefore: This is that reply, member by member — each with its own identifier, its own expiry and its own button, which is what the tokens table drew before it started grouping. The columns mean what
setIdNote: — this service's own handle on the reply. It is in no token, no client ever sees it, and it is not a claim: it exists so that a console page can say which credentials arrived together, which nothing in the protocol records.
setKeyNote: — a set of one has no issuance id, so this is the row's own handle in the issued register.
mixedNote: . The ordinary case rather than a fault: an access token and the refresh token issued with it have very different lifetimes.
sessionUnauthenticated: — nobody had authenticated on that session when this was issued.
noSession: none — this was issued with no browser sign-on session behind it, which is true of both direct grants, a pre-authorized code, every token exchange, and every assertion and ticket. A fact about the credential rather than a gap in the recording.
invalidateSetLead: One act rather than one click per credential, and it writes nowhere new: each member goes through the same revocation /oauth2/revoke performs, one at a time. What it saves is the mistake of revoking two of three and believing the grant is dead — a refresh token left behind mints a new access token, which is the whole reason a reply is worth being one row.
onlySomeRevocable: Only {n} of the {size} can be revoked; the rest are left alone.
restoreNonSpec: Restore is NON-SPEC and no real authorization server can offer it — a resource server may already have cached the refusal. It is here because getting back to a working token otherwise means restarting this service.
membersNote: In the order they were minted. Every identifier is a link to where that credential came from — who it was issued to, in whose name, to reach what, and every generation behind it if a token exchange or a refresh produced it. That lineage is a different relation from this page: this is what arrived together, and that is what one credential descends from. Refreshing this set produces a new set beside it, not a fourth member of it, and the lineage is what joins the two.
detailDisagrees: The Detail column will disagree with itself here, and that is by design. An access token's scope is what that token can do; the refresh token beside it carries what was authorized, which is wider whenever a scope became the audience — see the tokens page. A set that reported one scope would be hiding the one place the two halves of a grant deliberately differ.
